mentions.quote: The king, free from anger and greed, should look into legal disputes with learned Brāhmaṇas
mentions.role: presiding authority over legal disputes

mentions.quote: a Brāhmaṇa who knows all dharma should be appointed, along with the assessors
mentions.role: delegator of judicial authority

mentions.quote: A king, having found a treasure, should give half to Brāhmaṇas
mentions.role: duty-bound distributor of found treasure

mentions.quote: the king should have all ordeals performed in the presence of himself and of Brāhmaṇas
mentions.role: overseer of ordeals

mentions.quote: The king, having established a settlement in a town and settled Brāhmaṇas there
mentions.role: state founder and patron of Brāhmaṇas

entities.description: The sovereign ruler responsible for administering justice, adjudicating disputes, overseeing ordeals, and protecting subjects' property and welfare.
entities.justification: The king appears throughout the window as the central enforcer of dharma-based legal procedure, from appointing court assessors to conducting ordeals and settling inheritance disputes.

mentions.quote: The king, free from anger and greed, should look into legal disputes with learned Brāhmaṇas
mentions.role: legal advisors to the king

mentions.quote: False witnesses should be punished separately with a fine double the amount in dispute; a Brāhmaṇa, however, is to be banished
mentions.role: exempt from monetary punishment, banished instead

mentions.quote: A king, having found a treasure, should give half to Brāhmaṇas. If a Brāhmaṇa finds it, a learned one may take the whole
mentions.role: privileged recipient of treasure

mentions.quote: The sons of a Brāhmaṇa by wives of different varṇas shall have shares of four, three, two, and one, in order
mentions.role: head of varṇa-differentiated inheritance shares

mentions.quote: a Brāhmaṇa who knows all dharma should be appointed, along with the assessors
mentions.role: judicial proxy for absent king

entities.description: The priestly varna occupying the highest position in the fourfold social order, accorded special privileges in legal procedure, inheritance, ordeals, and the settlement of disputes.
entities.justification: Brāhmaṇas receive distinctive legal treatment throughout the chapter, including exemption from corporal punishment, preferred inheritance shares, and appointment as judges.

mentions.quote: in accordance with the Dharmaśāstra
mentions.role: normative legal authority invoked by the king

mentions.quote: Assessors who act contrary to Smṛti out of passion, greed, or fear
mentions.role: standard of judicial conduct

mentions.quote: it is the established rule that Dharmaśāstra is more powerful than Arthaśāstra
mentions.role: hierarchically superior normative text

entities.description: The body of sacred legal-moral literature (including Smṛtis) that provides the authoritative basis for judicial decisions and social conduct.
entities.justification: Dharmaśāstra is explicitly named as the source of legal authority superior to Arthaśāstra, and Smṛti is cited as the benchmark against which judicial misconduct is measured.

mentions.quote: it is the established rule that Dharmaśāstra is more powerful than Arthaśāstra
mentions.role: subordinate normative-political text

entities.description: The treatise on statecraft and political economy, acknowledged as a source of legal reasoning but subordinate to the Dharmaśāstra in normative authority.
entities.justification: The text explicitly ranks Arthaśāstra below Dharmaśāstra when the two conflict in legal matters, marking it as a recognized but secondary authority.

mentions.quote: Having made the accused utter the imprecation, 'O Varuṇa, protect me with truth,' he should enter the water
mentions.role: divine guardian invoked in the water ordeal

entities.description: The Vedic deity of cosmic order, truth, and waters, invoked during the ordeal by water as a divine witness and protector of truth.
entities.justification: Varuṇa is directly addressed in the ritual imprecation before the water ordeal, linking the deity to the juridical-cosmic function of upholding truth in legal proceedings.

mentions.quote: O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in the dharma of truth
mentions.role: divine progenitor of poison, associated with dharma and truth

entities.description: The creator deity in the Hindu triad, invoked as the divine origin of poison in the ritual imprecation of the ordeal by poison.
entities.justification: Brahmā is named as the progenitor of the poison used in the ordeal, framing the ordeal as a cosmologically grounded truth-testing mechanism.

mentions.quote: O Fire, you move within all beings, O Purifier. Like a witness to merit and sin, speak the truth to me, O wise one
mentions.role: divine witness to truth and sin in the fire ordeal

entities.description: Agni, the Vedic fire deity, invoked during the ordeal by fire as an omniscient witness to dharma, merit, and sin.
entities.justification: Fire is directly addressed in the ritualized speech before the ordeal, positioning it as a divine juridical witness present within all living beings.

mentions.quote: for its purification, a sacrificial porridge to Sarasvatī must be offered by the twice-born
mentions.role: deity to whom purificatory sacrifice is offered after false testimony

entities.description: The goddess of speech, knowledge, and wisdom, to whom a purificatory offering is prescribed for twice-born persons who have given false testimony to save a life.
entities.justification: Sarasvatī is explicitly named as the recipient of an expiatory porridge offering, signaling her connection to speech, testimony, and its ritual purification.

mentions.quote: O Balance, you are the abode of truth, created of old by the gods. Therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one
mentions.role: divinely created instrument of truth in the balance ordeal

mentions.quote: If I am a sinner, O Mother, then take me down; if I am pure, then carry me upwards
mentions.role: addressed as a maternal divine judge

entities.description: The weighing scale used in the ordeal by balance, addressed as a divine, truth-discerning entity created by the gods.
entities.justification: The balance is addressed with a direct invocation treating it as a divine sentient being whose movement reveals guilt or innocence, making it a ritually active judicial instrument.

mentions.quote: he should eat the Śārṅga poison from the Himalayan mountains; he whose body digests it without ill effects, his purity should be declared
mentions.role: substance used in ordeal by poison

entities.description: A specific poison sourced from the Himalayan mountains and used in the ordeal by poison to determine truth through bodily reaction.
entities.justification: Śārṅga poison from the Himalayas is named as the exact substance employed in the poison ordeal, and its digestion without harm proves the accused's innocence.

mentions.quote: he should eat the Śārṅga poison from the Himalayan mountains
mentions.role: geographic source of the ordeal poison

entities.description: The mountain range in northern India identified as the provenance of the Śārṅga poison used in the ordeal by poison.
entities.justification: The Himalayan mountains are explicitly cited as the origin of the specific poison prescribed for the ordeal, giving it geographical grounding.

mentions.quote: one should place seven Aśvattha leaves on them and wrap them with a thread
mentions.role: ritual material used in the fire ordeal preparation

entities.description: The sacred fig tree (Ficus religiosa), whose leaves are placed on the accused's hands as a ritual preparation for the fire ordeal.
entities.justification: Aśvattha leaves are specified by name as part of the ritual procedure for the fire ordeal, indicating their sacred protective or apotropaic role.

mentions.quote: the sons of a Kṣatriya, three, two, and one
mentions.role: second varna whose sons receive varṇa-differentiated inheritance shares

entities.description: The warrior-ruler varna, second in the fourfold social hierarchy, whose sons' inheritance shares are distributed proportionally across sub-varṇa unions.
entities.justification: Kṣatriyas are explicitly named alongside Brāhmaṇas and Vaiśyas in the rule for inheritance shares of sons born to fathers of these varṇas by wives of different classes.

mentions.quote: the sons of a Vaiśya, two and one
mentions.role: third varna in inheritance share distribution

entities.description: The merchant-cultivator varna, third in the fourfold social hierarchy, referenced in the proportional inheritance rules for sons of inter-varṇa unions.
entities.justification: Vaiśya is named in the inheritance-share verse as the third varṇa category whose sons receive shares in a two-to-one ratio.

mentions.quote: fire or water is for a Śūdra, or seven grains of poison
mentions.role: lowest varna assigned specific ordeal types

mentions.quote: Slavery is in the direct order of the varṇas, not in the reverse order
mentions.role: last in the varna order for permissible servitude

entities.description: The servant varna, lowest in the fourfold social hierarchy, who are assigned specific ordeal types and are the natural subject of the slavery rules.
entities.justification: Śūdras are distinguished by the ordeals prescribed for them (fire, water, or poison) and implicitly occupy the end-point of the varṇa-ordered slavery rule.

themes.topic: Procedural justice and the four-footed lawsuit

mentions.quote: This four-footed legal procedure is shown in disputes
The king, free from anger and greed, should look into legal disputes with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the Dharmaśāstra

themes.justification: The chapter opens by laying out a systematic legal procedure (plaint, reply, proof, judgment) as the normative framework for all dispute resolution.

themes.topic: Hierarchy of legal authority: Dharmaśāstra over Arthaśāstra over custom

mentions.quote: In a conflict between two Smṛtis, reason based on custom is stronger in legal matters. But it is the established rule that Dharmaśāstra is more powerful than Arthaśāstra

themes.justification: The text establishes an explicit normative hierarchy among legal sources, resolving conflicts between sacred law texts, political science texts, and custom.

mentions.quote: An eightieth part is the interest per month when there is a pledge; otherwise, it is two, three, four, or five percent, according to the order of the varṇas
A debt contracted for the sake of the family by undivided members must be paid by the heirs when the head of the family is dead

themes.justification: A major section of the chapter is devoted to detailed rules on interest rates, debt recovery, suretyship, and the transmission of debt obligations across generations.

mentions.quote: The balance, fire, water, poison, and sacred libation are the ordeals here for purification
O Balance, you are the abode of truth, created of old by the gods. Therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one

themes.justification: The ordeal section frames natural and crafted substances as divinely animated truth-detectors, blending ritual theology with judicial procedure.

mentions.quote: False witnesses should be punished separately with a fine double the amount in dispute; a Brāhmaṇa, however, is to be banished
fire or water is for a Śūdra, or seven grains of poison
it is two, three, four, or five percent, according to the order of the varṇas

themes.justification: Throughout the chapter, legal penalties, interest rates, ordeal types, and inheritance shares vary systematically by varṇa, embedding caste hierarchy into the legal code.

themes.topic: Inheritance, partition, and the twelve types of sons

mentions.quote: The aurasa is born of a lawful wife; equal to him is the putrikāsuta, the son of an appointed daughter. The kṣetraja is one begotten on the wife's field by a kinsman
After the death of the parents, the sons should divide the assets and debts equally

themes.justification: A substantial portion of the chapter enumerates twelve recognized categories of sons and their respective inheritance entitlements, reflecting the legal importance of patrilineal succession.

themes.topic: Strīdhana (women's property) and marital property rights

mentions.quote: What is given by the father, mother, husband, or brother, what is received at the nuptial fire, and the gift on supersession and the like, is declared to be strīdhana
The strīdhana of a childless woman married in one of the four forms beginning with the Brāhma goes to her husband

themes.justification: The text systematically defines strīdhana, its various sources, and its transmission rules upon death or marriage dissolution, marking women's property as a distinct legal category.

mentions.quote: Proof is declared to be a document, possession, and witnesses
When any matter is settled by mutual consent, a document with witnesses should be made, on which the creditor's name is written first

themes.justification: The chapter gives extensive attention to the preparation, authentication, and evidentiary weight of written documents in legal proceedings, reflecting an emerging legal formalism.

themes.topic: Truth, perjury, and karmic consequences of false testimony

mentions.quote: Whatever worlds are for those who commit sins and for those who commit great sins
Whatever merit you have acquired in hundreds of past lives, know that all of it goes to him whom you falsely cause to be defeated

themes.justification: The witness section frames perjury not merely as a legal offense but as a karmically catastrophic act, invoking the loss of accumulated merit across lifetimes.

themes.topic: Property, possession, and the limits of prescriptive rights

mentions.quote: The loss of land occurs after twenty years of it being enjoyed by another while the owner looks on without protest
Title is superior to possession, unless the possession has come down through successive generations

themes.justification: The chapter develops a nuanced doctrine of title versus possession, including prescriptive periods and exceptions, reflecting sophisticated thinking about property rights.

mentions.quote: Corporations, guilds, and families, when authorized by the king, are to be known as successively more authoritative in the administration of justice for men
This same rule applies to guilds, corporations, heretical sects, and other associations; the king should protect them from one another

themes.justification: The text implicitly recognizes guilds, corporations, and associations as legally constituted bodies with their own authority structures nested within royal sovereignty.

themes.topic: Ritual purification and the sacred grounding of legal acts

mentions.quote: for its purification, a sacrificial porridge to Sarasvatī must be offered by the twice-born
O Fire, you move within all beings, O Purifier. Like a witness to merit and sin, speak the truth to me, O wise one

themes.justification: The chapter implicitly treats certain legal violations (false testimony, necessary lies) as ritual impurities requiring sacrificial atonement, not merely civic penalties.

citations.justification: The Dharmaśāstra is invoked as the primary normative authority governing the king's conduct of legal proceedings.

citations.quote: it is the established rule that Dharmaśāstra is more powerful than Arthaśāstra
citations.justification: The Arthaśāstra is cited as a recognized but subordinate legal authority in cases of conflict with Dharmaśāstra.
